units.title: Artılar ve eksiler
units.description: Bir konunun lehine ve aleyhine gerekçeli bir deneme yazmak
units.guide:
## Bu ünitede yapabileceklerin
- Bir tartışmada iki tarafın gerekçelerini dinleyerek ayırt edebilirsin.
- Bir köşe yazısında yazarın tutumunu ve gerekçelerini bulabilirsin.
- Bir konunun artılarını ve eksilerini bir dakikada dengeli biçimde anlatabilirsin.
- Giriş, iki görüş ve sonuçtan oluşan 180–220 kelimelik bir deneme yazabilirsin.

## Strateji
- Gölgeleme (shadowing) yaparken **on the one hand / on the other hand** gibi geçiş ifadelerini vurgulayarak tekrar et; konuşurken de aynı ritmi kullan.
- Önce-dinle hikâyesinde metni açmadan iki sütun not al: **lehte** ve **aleyhte**. Her konuşmacının hangi tarafta olduğunu yaz, sonra metni açıp kontrol et.
- Köşe yazısında yazarın görüşü genellikle son paragraflarda gelir: **I have come to…**, **In my view…** gibi ifadeleri ara.
- Denemeden önce plan yap: her görüş için iki gerekçe ve bir örnek. Sonuçta yeni bir gerekçe ekleme, kendi görüşünü söyle.

## Model metin
> Should employees be allowed to work from home? Since the pandemic, more and more companies have had to answer this question, and there are strong arguments on both sides.
>
> On the one hand, working from home saves time and money. Employees who do not have to commute for hours are often more relaxed and productive. Many people also say that they can concentrate better in a quiet room than in a busy open-plan office. In addition, companies that offer flexible arrangements find it easier to keep their best staff.
>
> On the other hand, there are serious disadvantages. New employees learn a great deal by watching experienced colleagues, and this is difficult on a video call. Moreover, not every job can be done remotely. Drivers, nurses and shop assistants have to be at work, so a home-working policy may seem unfair to them. Some people also feel lonely when they rarely see their team.
>
> In conclusion, I believe that a hybrid model is the best solution. If employees spend two or three days in the office, they can learn from each other and still enjoy the benefits of working from home. However, each company should test the idea before making it permanent.

Dört paragraf: soru ile açılan giriş, **On the one hand** ile lehte görüşler, **On the other hand** ile aleyhte görüşler ve **In conclusion** ile kendi görüşün. Paragraf içinde **In addition**, **Moreover** gibi bağlayıcılarla gerekçe ekle.

## Türklerin sık hatası
- ❌ The technology changed the working life. ✅ **Technology** has changed **working life**. (Genel bir şeyden söz ederken **the** kullanma.)
- ❌ It has a positive effect to productivity. / We discussed about it. ✅ It has a positive effect **on** productivity. / We **discussed** it. (Eşdizimleri kalıp olarak öğren: effect on, arguments on both sides, discuss + nesne.)

exercises.passage:
Four Days, Full Pay: Too Good to Be True?

Last month, a small design agency in Kadıköy announced that its staff would work four days a week for the same salary. Within a week, the agency had received more than two hundred job applications. Unsurprisingly, other employers have started asking whether they should follow its example.

Supporters of the four-day week make a persuasive case. They argue that people who are well rested make fewer mistakes and are less likely to quit. In a trial carried out in several British companies, most managers reported that productivity stayed the same, while sick days fell sharply. Supporters also point out that a shorter week could reduce traffic, which is no small advantage in a city like Istanbul.

Critics, however, are not convinced. Not every job can be squeezed into four days, they say. A café cannot serve customers on a day it is closed, and a logistics firm cannot tell its clients that parcels will only be delivered from Monday to Thursday. In such businesses, the fifth day would have to be covered by extra staff, and somebody would have to pay for them. Critics also warn that longer working days may simply leave employees more exhausted than before.

Having spoken to people on both sides, I have come to a cautious conclusion. The four-day week is not a magic solution, but it should not be dismissed as a fantasy either. Had the Kadıköy agency introduced the change without consulting its team, it might well have failed. Instead, its managers spent three months testing different schedules and asking staff for feedback. That, rather than the number of days, may be the real lesson.

Perhaps the question we should be asking is not "four days or five?" but "how do we measure good work?" If companies judged their staff by results rather than by hours spent at a desk, the debate might look very different. Until then, I suspect most of us will keep checking our emails on Fridays.

nodes.title: Ofis mi, ev mi?
nodes.description: Merkez Maslak'a taşınınca Deniz'in ekibi evden çalışmayı tartışıyor

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Thanks for staying, everyone. Since we moved to Maslak, I've had a lot of complaints about the commute.
steps.translation: Kaldığınız için teşekkürler. Maslak'a taşındığımızdan beri yol konusunda çok şikâyet aldım.

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: Not surprising. Some people now spend three hours a day in traffic. That's fifteen hours a week.
steps.translation: Şaşırtıcı değil. Bazıları artık günde üç saat trafikte geçiriyor. Bu da haftada on beş saat demek.

steps.speaker: Kerem
steps.text: My team has a suggestion. Let people work from home two days a week, say Tuesdays and Thursdays.
steps.translation: Ekibimin bir önerisi var. İnsanlar haftada iki gün evden çalışsın, mesela salı ve perşembe.

steps.prompt: Kerem'in ekibi haftada kaç gün evden çalışmayı öneriyor?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Before we decide, let's look at both sides. Kerem, what are the main advantages?
steps.translation: Karar vermeden önce iki tarafa da bakalım. Kerem, başlıca avantajlar neler?

steps.speaker: Kerem
steps.text: First, people would get those hours back. Second, developers need quiet time to write good code.
steps.translation: Birincisi, insanlar o saatleri geri kazanır. İkincisi, yazılımcıların iyi kod yazmak için sessiz zamana ihtiyacı var.

steps.speaker: Kerem
steps.text: If we had had a quieter office last month, that update might have been tested properly.
steps.translation: Geçen ay daha sessiz bir ofisimiz olsaydı, o güncelleme düzgünce test edilmiş olabilirdi.

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: Hmm, I'm not sure the office was the problem. But go on.
steps.translation: Hımm, sorunun ofis olduğundan emin değilim. Ama devam et.

steps.speaker: Kerem
steps.text: And third, we'd keep our people. Two engineers have already been offered jobs closer to home.
steps.translation: Üçüncüsü de insanlarımızı elde tutarız. İki mühendise evlerine daha yakın işler çoktan teklif edildi.

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: That's a serious point. Losing them would cost us far more than a few empty desks.
steps.translation: Bu ciddi bir nokta. Onları kaybetmek bize birkaç boş masadan çok daha pahalıya patlar.

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: Maybe, but empty desks aren't the only cost. Teams that never meet tend to stop talking to each other.
steps.translation: Olabilir ama tek maliyet boş masalar değil. Hiç bir araya gelmeyen ekipler birbiriyle konuşmayı bırakma eğiliminde.

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Selin, you look unconvinced. What are the disadvantages?
steps.translation: Selin, ikna olmamış görünüyorsun. Dezavantajlar neler?

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: My biggest worry is the new staff. Since the merger, we've hired twelve people, and most of them are juniors.
steps.translation: En büyük endişem yeni çalışanlar. Birleşmeden beri on iki kişi işe aldık ve çoğu yeni başlayan.

steps.prompt: Birleşmeden beri kaç kişi işe alındı?

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: They learn by listening to experienced colleagues. You can't pick that up on a video call.
steps.translation: Deneyimli meslektaşlarını dinleyerek öğreniyorlar. Bunu görüntülü bir görüşmede kapamazsın.

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: And our drivers and warehouse staff can't work from home at all. It might seem unfair to them.
steps.translation: Ayrıca sürücülerimiz ve depo çalışanlarımız hiç evden çalışamaz. Bu onlara haksızlık gibi görünebilir.

steps.speaker: Kerem
steps.text: That's a valid point. I hadn't thought about the warehouse team.
steps.translation: Haklı bir nokta. Depo ekibini düşünmemiştim.

steps.prompt: Kerem, Selin'in depo çalışanlarıyla ilgili görüşüne nasıl tepki veriyor?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: So, on the one hand, we'd save time and keep our engineers. On the other hand, juniors and drivers might lose out.
steps.translation: Yani bir yandan zaman kazanır ve mühendislerimizi tutarız. Öte yandan yeni başlayanlar ve sürücüler kayıplı çıkabilir.

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: What if we tried it for three months? New staff would come in every day during their first month.
steps.translation: Peki üç ay denesek? Yeni çalışanlar ilk aylarında her gün gelir.

steps.speaker: Kerem
steps.text: And the warehouse could get something too, like flexible start times. Would that work, Selin?
steps.translation: Depo da bir şey kazanabilir, esnek başlama saatleri gibi. Bu işe yarar mı Selin?

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: It might. I'd want to see the numbers first: delays, mistakes and how many people leave.
steps.translation: Yarayabilir. Önce rakamları görmek isterim: gecikmeler, hatalar ve kaç kişinin ayrıldığı.

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Fair enough. Kerem, could you have your team put together a short proposal by Friday?
steps.translation: Makul. Kerem, ekibine cumaya kadar kısa bir öneri hazırlatabilir misin?

steps.speaker: Kerem
steps.text: Sure. And I'll ask Mia whether she'd write about it. Her readers love this topic.
steps.translation: Tabii. Mia'ya da bu konuda yazıp yazmayacağını sorarım. Okurları bu konuya bayılıyor.

steps.prompt: "Her readers love this topic" cümlesindeki "her" kimi anlatıyor?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Let's not go public yet. We had enough headlines after the system crashed!
steps.translation: Henüz kamuoyuna açıklamayalım. Sistem çöktükten sonra yeterince manşet olduk!

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: Agreed. A three-month trial, a proposal by Friday, and no articles until we see results.
steps.translation: Anlaştık. Üç aylık bir deneme, cumaya kadar bir öneri ve sonuçları görene kadar makale yok.

units.description: Bir sunum ya da podcastten not alıp ana noktaları özetlemek
units.guide:
## Bu ünitede yapabileceklerin
- 3–4 dakikalık bir podcast ya da sunumdan ana fikri ve ana noktaları not alabilirsin.
- Konuşmacının konu değiştirdiğini haber veren ifadeleri (that brings me to…, to sum up…) yakalayabilirsin.
- Bir konuşmanın yazılı özetinde yazarın tutumunu ve çıkarımlarını bulabilirsin.
- Notlarından yaklaşık 120 kelimelik bir özet yazabilir ve konuşmayı bir arkadaşına aktarabilirsin.

## Strateji
- Önce-dinle hikâyesinde metni açmadan sadece anahtar kelimeleri yaz: sayılar, saatler, **first / second / finally** sonrası gelen fikirler. Tam cümle yazmaya çalışma.
- Konuşmacı **The main point…**, **That brings me to…**, **If there's one thing…** dediğinde kulak kabart: önemli bilgi hemen arkadan gelir.
- Gölgeleme (shadowing) ile aktarma kalıplarını (**The speaker argued that…**) ağzına yerleştir; özetlerken bu kalıplar hazır olsun.
- Dictogloss: dinle, not al, notlardan metni yeniden kur, sonra orijinalle karşılaştır. Amaç birebir kopya değil, aynı bilgiyi doğru dille vermek.

## Model metin
> In a recent episode of the podcast Istanbul at Work, Deniz from RotaLojistik talked about the day the company's tracking system crashed. The problem started at six in the morning, and more than two thousand deliveries were delayed. Deniz explained that the cause was a software update which had not been tested properly.
>
> Deniz argued that the company had learned three lessons. First, speed should never become more important than safety. Second, it is better to tell clients the truth immediately than to stay silent. The company issued a statement before noon and lost only one client. Finally, every system should be checked by people who did not build it.
>
> The main message was that mistakes are unavoidable, but companies must admit them quickly and learn from them.

Üç paragraf: konuşma ve olay, üç ders (**First, Second, Finally**) ve tek cümlelik ana mesaj. Geçmiş olaylar aktarılırken zaman geriye kayar: **was not tested → had not been tested**.

## Türklerin sık hatası
- ❌ Deniz said me that the update didn't test. ✅ Deniz **told me** / **said** that the update **had not been tested**. (say + that, tell + kişi; edilgen ve zaman kaydırma.)
- ❌ Number of delayed deliveries was over two thousand. ✅ **The** number of delayed deliveries was over two thousand. (Belirli bir şeyden söz ederken **the**; "a number of" ise "birçok" demektir.)

Notes from the Istanbul Logistics Summit
by Selin, RotaLojistik

The talk that everybody was discussing at lunch on Thursday was not given by a famous CEO. It was given by Dr Aylin Erdem, a researcher who has spent ten years studying how companies behave during a crisis.

Her message was surprisingly simple: customers forgive mistakes far more easily than they forgive silence. To prove it, she described an experiment in which two groups of online shoppers were told that their parcels would arrive three days late. The first group received a short, honest explanation and an apology within an hour. The second group heard nothing until the parcels finally arrived. A month later, the first group were twice as likely to order again.

Dr Erdem then went on to explain why so many companies still choose to stay quiet. According to her research, managers are usually afraid of two things: admitting that something has gone wrong before they know the cause, and promising a solution they cannot deliver. "Both fears are understandable," she said, "but customers do not expect you to have every answer. They expect you to tell them what you know and when they will hear from you again."

The most practical part of the talk came at the end. She recommended that every company prepare a "first-hour message" in advance: a short statement that can be sent the moment a problem is noticed. It should say what has happened, who is affected and when the next update will be given, and nothing more.

I have to admit that I was sceptical at first. Some of her figures came from small studies, and logistics is not the same as online fashion. Still, I left the room convinced that we had been lucky last month. Had we waited until the afternoon to speak to our clients, we might have lost far more than one contract. I will be suggesting a first-hour message at our next team meeting.

nodes.description: Mia'nın podcastinde Deniz sistem çöküşünden çıkan dersleri anlatıyor

steps.speaker: Mia
steps.text: Welcome back to Istanbul at Work, the podcast about the people behind the city's businesses. I'm Mia.
steps.translation: Istanbul at Work'e tekrar hoş geldiniz; şehrin işletmelerinin arkasındaki insanları anlatan podcast. Ben Mia.

steps.speaker: Mia
steps.text: My guest today runs operations at RotaLojistik, whose tracking system crashed last month. Deniz, welcome.
steps.translation: Bugünkü konuğum, takip sistemi geçen ay çöken RotaLojistik'in operasyonlarını yönetiyor. Deniz, hoş geldin.

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Thanks, Mia. I'm happy to talk about it now. A month ago, I'd have said no!
steps.translation: Teşekkürler Mia. Artık bunu konuşmaktan memnunum. Bir ay önce hayır derdim!

steps.speaker: Mia
steps.text: Let's start with the day itself. What actually happened?
steps.translation: O günün kendisiyle başlayalım. Aslında ne oldu?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: At six in the morning, our tracking system went down. Drivers couldn't see their routes, and customers couldn't see their parcels.
steps.translation: Sabah altıda takip sistemimiz çöktü. Sürücüler rotalarını, müşteriler de kolilerini göremiyordu.

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: By eight o'clock, more than two thousand deliveries had been delayed, and our phones didn't stop ringing.
steps.translation: Saat sekize kadar iki binden fazla teslimat gecikmişti ve telefonlarımız susmak bilmedi.

steps.speaker: Mia
steps.text: And the cause was a software update, wasn't it?
steps.translation: Sebebi de bir yazılım güncellemesiydi, değil mi?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Yes. It had been installed the night before, and it hadn't been tested properly. That was our mistake, not the software's.
steps.translation: Evet. Bir önceki gece kurulmuştu ve düzgünce test edilmemişti. Bu yazılımın değil, bizim hatamızdı.

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: So the first lesson I'd like to share is simple: never let speed become more important than safety.
steps.translation: Paylaşmak istediğim ilk ders basit: hızın güvenlikten daha önemli hâle gelmesine asla izin verme.

steps.speaker: Mia
steps.text: That's easy to say, but hard to do in a start-up, isn't it?
steps.translation: Söylemesi kolay ama bir girişimde yapması zor, değil mi?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Absolutely. Start-ups are always in a hurry. But had we waited one more day, we would have saved a fortune.
steps.translation: Kesinlikle. Girişimler hep acele eder. Ama bir gün daha bekleseydik, bir servet kurtarmış olurduk.

steps.speaker: Mia
steps.text: What was the second lesson?
steps.translation: İkinci ders neydi?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Communication. Our instinct was to stay quiet until everything was fixed. Luckily, a colleague persuaded us to do the opposite.
steps.translation: İletişim. İçgüdümüz her şey düzelene kadar sessiz kalmaktı. Neyse ki bir meslektaşımız bizi tam tersini yapmaya ikna etti.

steps.speaker: Mia
steps.text: Why was staying quiet such a bad idea?
steps.translation: Sessiz kalmak neden bu kadar kötü bir fikirdi?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Because clients imagine the worst when you say nothing. Silence looks like you're hiding something.
steps.translation: Çünkü hiçbir şey söylemezsen müşteriler en kötüsünü düşünür. Sessizlik bir şey saklıyormuşsun gibi görünür.

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: We issued a statement before noon, apologised, and promised compensation. Most clients told us they appreciated the honesty.
steps.translation: Öğleden önce bir açıklama yaptık, özür diledik ve tazminat sözü verdik. Müşterilerin çoğu dürüstlüğü takdir ettiklerini söyledi.

steps.speaker: Mia
steps.text: Did you lose any clients?
steps.translation: Hiç müşteri kaybettiniz mi?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Only one, and frankly, it had been unhappy with us for a while. Two others actually increased their orders.
steps.translation: Sadece bir tane; açıkçası o da bir süredir bizden memnun değildi. Diğer iki müşteri ise siparişlerini artırdı.

steps.prompt: "it had been unhappy with us for a while" cümlesindeki "it" neyi anlatıyor?

steps.speaker: Mia
steps.text: Interesting. And the third lesson?
steps.translation: İlginç. Peki üçüncü ders?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Have your systems checked by people who didn't build them. Now every update is tested twice, once by an outside team.
steps.translation: Sistemlerini, onları yapmamış kişilere kontrol ettir. Artık her güncelleme iki kez test ediliyor, bir kez de dışarıdan bir ekip tarafından.

steps.speaker: Mia
steps.text: Some listeners might say that sounds expensive.
steps.translation: Bazı dinleyiciler bunun pahalı göründüğünü söyleyebilir.

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: It is expensive. But it's far cheaper than another morning like that one. I'd make the same decision again tomorrow.
steps.translation: Pahalı. Ama öyle bir sabahı yeniden yaşamaktan çok daha ucuz. Yarın yine aynı kararı verirdim.

steps.prompt: Deniz, dışarıdan test ettirmenin maliyeti hakkında ne düşünüyor?

steps.speaker: Mia
steps.text: Finally, what would you say to other managers listening today?
steps.translation: Son olarak, bugün bizi dinleyen diğer yöneticilere ne söylersin?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Mistakes will happen. What matters is how quickly you admit them and what you change afterwards.
steps.translation: Hatalar olacak. Önemli olan onları ne kadar çabuk kabul ettiğin ve sonrasında neyi değiştirdiğin.

steps.speaker: Mia
steps.text: Deniz from RotaLojistik, thank you. After the break: why so many cafés in Kadıköy are hiring delivery riders.
steps.translation: RotaLojistik'ten Deniz, teşekkürler. Aradan sonra: Kadıköy'deki pek çok kafe neden kurye işe alıyor?

In a recent episode of the podcast Istanbul at Work, Deniz from RotaLojistik talked about the day the company's tracking system crashed. The problem started at six in the morning, and more than two thousand deliveries were delayed. Deniz explained that the cause was a software update which had not been tested properly.

The main message was that mistakes are unavoidable, but companies must admit them quickly and learn from them.

units.title: Toplantıda ikna
units.description: Bir öneri sunmak, itirazları karşılamak ve teklif e-postası yazmak
units.guide:
## Bu ünitede yapabileceklerin
- Toplantıda bir öneriyi gerekçeleriyle sunabilirsin.
- Bir itirazı kabul edip sakin ve somut bir yanıtla karşılayabilirsin.
- Bir makalede itirazlarla ilgili tavsiyeleri ve yazarın tutumunu bulabilirsin.
- Yaklaşık 150 kelimelik resmî bir teklif e-postası yazabilirsin.

## Strateji
- Gölgeleme (shadowing) yaparken **I completely understand your concern** gibi kalıpları sakin ve yavaş bir tonla tekrar et; toplantıda ses tonun da ikna eder.
- Önce-dinle hikâyesinde her itirazı ve Deniz'in ona verdiği yanıtı eşleştirerek not al: maliyet → pilot, kayıp koli → tarama, çıkar çatışması → herkese aynı koşullar.
- Önerini üç adımda sun: sorun (rakamla), çözüm, karşı tarafın kazancı. İtiraz gelince önce teşekkür et, sonra asıl endişeyi yanıtla.
- Teklif e-postasında bir paragraf, bir iş: öneri, faydalar, itiraza yanıt ve kibar kapanış.

## Model metin
> Subject: Proposal: pick-up points at your cafés
>
> Dear Elif,
>
> Thank you for meeting me last week. As promised, I am writing to propose a three-month pilot scheme in which your two cafés would become RotaLojistik pick-up points.
>
> At the moment, almost one in five of our parcels cannot be delivered on the first attempt. If customers could collect them from your cafés, we would save time and money, and you would gain new visitors, many of whom are likely to order a coffee. We would also pay you a fee of ten lira for every parcel.
>
> I understand that space behind the counter is limited. For this reason, we would provide a small shelf and a scanner, so every parcel could be tracked at all times. If the pilot does not work for you, you can end it with two weeks' notice.
>
> I would be happy to discuss the details at your convenience.
>
> Best regards,
> Deniz

Konu satırı öneriyi söylüyor. İlk paragraf öneriyi, ikincisi iki tarafın kazancını, üçüncüsü olası itirazı (yer sorunu) ve çözümünü veriyor. Kapanış resmî ve kısa.

## Türklerin sık hatası
- ❌ I would be happy to discuss about the details. ✅ I would be happy to **discuss the details**. (discuss doğrudan nesne alır; ama talk **about**.)
- ❌ I suggest you to start a pilot. ✅ I suggest **starting** a pilot. / I suggest **that we start** a pilot. (suggest + kişi + to kullanılmaz.)

## Beceri testi
Bölüm 7 beceri testi 20 sorudur; geçmek için %80 doğru yap. Bölümün **tamamlandı** sayılması için bu testi ve bu ünitenin yazma görevini (teklif e-postası, l4) birlikte bitirmen gerekir.

| Bölüm | Soru | Ölçtüğü hedef |
|---|---|---|
| Dinleme | 6 | Geçmişi değerlendirme: third conditional (s7u1), perfect modals (s7u3); haber dili (s7u4); yaptırmak (s7u7); inversion (s7u8); toplantıda soru sorma (s7u15) |
| Okuma | 8 | Lehte-aleyhte köşe yazısı ve yazarın görüşü (s7u13, s7u10); toplantı sonrası güncelleme e-postası: aktarılan sözler ve kararlar (s7u14, s7u5, s7u15) |
| Yazma | 4 | Kriz değerlendirme (s7u12, s7u1); tutanakta aktarılan soru (s7u6); yaptırmak (s7u7); itirazı karşılayan öneri (s7u15) |
| Dil | 2 | Eşdizim: insist on (s7u9); kibar itiraz (s7u10, s7u15) |

exercises.passage:
Why Good Ideas Die in Meetings

Most proposals are not rejected because they are bad. They are rejected because the person presenting them treats every objection as an attack. In my twenty years of training managers, I have watched brilliant ideas disappear within minutes simply because someone became defensive.

The first rule is to welcome objections rather than fear them. A colleague who raises a concern is, in fact, telling you what you need to fix before the idea can succeed. Thanking that person, and meaning it, changes the atmosphere in the room immediately. Silence is far more dangerous: people who say nothing in a meeting often say a great deal in the corridor afterwards.

The second rule is to separate the concern from the conclusion. When a finance director says, "This is too expensive," the real question is usually "What happens if it fails?" Answer that question, not the first one. Offering a small pilot with clear limits on time and money often reassures people far more than any number of optimistic forecasts.

Third, never claim more than your evidence allows. Nothing destroys trust faster than a figure that turns out to be wrong. If you are not sure, say so, and promise to come back with the data. Rarely will anyone criticise you for being honest about what you do not know.

Finally, know what you are willing to give up. A proposal that cannot be changed is not a proposal; it is a demand. Before the meeting, decide which parts of your plan are essential and which can be negotiated. That way, you can make concessions without losing the heart of the idea.

None of this is complicated, yet I still see experienced professionals ignore it. Perhaps that is because handling objections well requires something harder than technique: the humility to accept that other people may see what you have missed.

nodes.title: Kafede teslim noktası
nodes.description: Deniz kafeleri teslim noktasına dönüştürmeyi öneriyor, Selin ve Kerem itiraz ediyor

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Thanks for coming. I'd like to propose something that could cut our failed deliveries in half.
steps.translation: Geldiğiniz için teşekkürler. Başarısız teslimatlarımızı yarıya indirebilecek bir şey önermek istiyorum.

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: In half? That's a bold claim. Go on, we're listening.
steps.translation: Yarıya mı? İddialı bir söz. Devam et, dinliyoruz.

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Right now, almost one in five parcels can't be delivered because nobody's at home. Every redelivery costs us money.
steps.translation: Şu anda kolilerin neredeyse beşte biri evde kimse olmadığı için teslim edilemiyor. Her yeniden teslimat bize para kaybettiriyor.

steps.prompt: Deniz'e göre şu an kolilerin ne kadarı teslim edilemiyor?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: My proposal is to turn local cafés into pick-up points. Customers would collect their parcels whenever it suits them.
steps.translation: Önerim, yerel kafeleri teslim noktalarına dönüştürmek. Müşteriler kolilerini kendilerine uygun olduğu zaman alırlar.

steps.speaker: Kerem
steps.text: Cafés? Why would a café owner want boxes piled up behind the counter?
steps.translation: Kafeler mi? Bir kafe sahibi neden tezgâhın arkasında kutuların yığılmasını istesin?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Because every customer who collects a parcel is likely to buy a coffee. We'd also pay a small fee per parcel.
steps.translation: Çünkü koli almaya gelen her müşteri büyük ihtimalle bir kahve alır. Ayrıca koli başına küçük bir ücret öderiz.

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: I'm not convinced. What if a parcel goes missing? Our brand would be damaged, not the café's.
steps.translation: İkna olmadım. Ya bir koli kaybolursa? Zarar gören kafenin değil, bizim markamız olur.

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: That's a fair concern. Every parcel would be scanned on arrival and again when it's collected, so we'd always know where it is.
steps.translation: Haklı bir endişe. Her koli gelişte ve teslim alınırken yeniden taranır; böylece nerede olduğunu her zaman biliriz.

steps.prompt: "so we'd always know where it is" cümlesindeki "it" neyi anlatıyor?

steps.speaker: Kerem
steps.text: That means new scanners and changes to the app. My team is already busy with the new testing process.
steps.translation: Bu, yeni tarayıcılar ve uygulamada değişiklik demek. Ekibim zaten yeni test süreciyle meşgul.

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: I understand. That's why I'm suggesting a small pilot first: two cafés, three months and a simple scanner.
steps.translation: Anlıyorum. Bu yüzden önce küçük bir pilot öneriyorum: iki kafe, üç ay ve basit bir tarayıcı.

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: If it doesn't work, we'll have lost very little. If it does, we'll have a model we can copy across the city.
steps.translation: İşe yaramazsa çok az şey kaybetmiş oluruz. Yararsa, şehrin her yerinde kopyalayabileceğimiz bir modelimiz olur.

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: And which two cafés did you have in mind?
steps.translation: Peki aklında hangi iki kafe var?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Elif's two cafés, the original one and the new Kadıköy branch. Both are on busy streets, and Elif has already shown interest.
steps.translation: Elif'in iki kafesi: ilki ve yeni Kadıköy şubesi. İkisi de işlek caddelerde ve Elif zaten ilgi gösterdi.

steps.speaker: Kerem
steps.text: Hold on, isn't that a conflict of interest? Elif is a client and a friend.
steps.translation: Bir dakika, bu bir çıkar çatışması değil mi? Elif hem müşteri hem arkadaş.

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Fair point. That's exactly why the terms would be the same for any café that joins later. Everything will be in writing.
steps.translation: Haklısın. Tam da bu yüzden koşullar sonradan katılacak her kafe için aynı olur. Her şey yazılı olacak.

steps.prompt: Deniz, Kerem'in çıkar çatışması itirazına nasıl yanıt veriyor?

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: What would success look like after three months?
steps.translation: Üç ay sonra başarı neye benzer?

steps.speaker: Deniz
steps.text: Fewer second attempts, at least two hundred parcels collected a month, and no lost items. I'll report the figures every month.
steps.translation: Daha az ikinci deneme, ayda en az iki yüz koli teslimi ve hiç kayıp yok. Rakamları her ay raporlarım.

steps.prompt: Başarı için ayda en az kaç kolinin teslim alınması gerekiyor?

steps.speaker: Selin
steps.text: All right. I still have doubts about the brand, but a pilot is a reasonable risk.

Dear Elif,

Thank you for meeting me last week. As promised, I am writing to propose a three-month pilot scheme in which your two cafés would become RotaLojistik pick-up points.

I understand that space behind the counter is limited. For this reason, we would provide a small shelf and a scanner, so every parcel could be tracked at all times. If the pilot does not work for you, you can end it with two weeks' notice.

I would be happy to discuss the details at your convenience.

Best regards,
Deniz

exercises.passage:
Should Delivery Robots Be Allowed on Our Pavements?

Small delivery robots have been tested in several European cities, and a trial is now being planned in Istanbul. Supporters argue that the robots could reduce traffic, because fewer vans would be needed for short trips. They also point out that robots can work at night, when roads are quiet, and that they produce no exhaust fumes.

Opponents are less enthusiastic. Pavements in many neighbourhoods are already narrow and crowded, and they worry that robots would make life even harder for wheelchair users and parents with pushchairs. Some shopkeepers also fear that their own delivery riders would lose their jobs.

In my view, both sides make valid points, but the debate is happening too early. Not a single robot has yet been tested on a steep, busy street like the ones in Beyoğlu. Until such a test has been carried out, any decision would be based on guesses rather than evidence. The city should therefore allow a limited trial in one district, publish the results, and only then decide whether the robots deserve a place on our pavements.

Subject: Café pick-up pilot: update

Hi everyone,

Here is a quick update on Deniz's proposal to turn local cafés into pick-up points.

At Monday's meeting, I said that I was worried about our brand, and Kerem was worried about the new scanners and the extra work for his team. Both concerns have now been answered. The scanners will be paid for from the marketing budget, since the pilot is partly an advertising campaign, and every parcel will be tracked from the moment it arrives at a café.

Elif has agreed to take part, but only on one condition: the shelf must not block the window. She told Deniz that she had already lost customers once when building work hid the café from the street, and she did not want it to happen again. Deniz has had a narrower shelf designed, so this should not be a problem.

The pilot will start in the second week of March and last three months. If fewer than two hundred parcels are collected in a month, we will review the scheme.

I have to admit I was against this idea at first. I am still cautious, but I think it deserves a fair chance.

Best,
Selin
